**The Museum of Small Things**

There is a museum I visit almost every day. It has no building, no ticket booth, no velvet ropes. It opens whenever I stop rushing. Its collection is made of moments most people would throw away.

This morning, the exhibit was a puddle. It had rained overnight, and the sidewalk held a shallow mirror. A single leaf floated in it, spinning slowly like a stalled planet. The sky in the puddle was not the same sky overhead; it was softer, older, slightly bruised by the branches. I stood there for maybe thirty seconds. In that time, a man with a briefcase stepped around me, a dog pulled its owner forward, a bus sighed at the corner. No one else looked down. But I had been to the museum.

I used to think attention was a resource, something to spend wisely. Now I think it is closer to a place. You can live in it, or you can pass through it. Most of us pass through. We scroll, we skim, we multitask, we call it efficiency. But efficiency is a terrible religion. It asks us to ignore the world in order to get through it. And the world, stubbornly, keeps offering itself anyway: the smell of rain on hot concrete, the way a stranger’s laugh catches in their throat, the blue hour just before streetlights come on.

Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I think she was right, but I would add that it is also a form of rebellion. To pay attention is to refuse the narrative that only big things matter. It is to say that a cracked tile, a child’s question, a sentence in an old book, a friend’s tired eyes are not interruptions. They are the thing itself.

I have a friend who collects abandoned grocery lists. She finds them in carts, on shelves, in the street. She says they are tiny autobiographies. *Milk, eggs, batteries, cat food, something for dinner that doesn’t take long.* You can learn a lot about a person from what they meant to buy. You can learn even more from what they crossed out. I love that she does this. It is not useful. It will never appear on a résumé. But it makes the world larger.

Maybe that is what I want to say: the world is already large. We are the ones who shrink it. We shrink it with hurry, with habit, with the assumption that we already know what we are looking at. But we don’t. A tree is not just a tree. It is a slow explosion of water and light. A stranger is not just a stranger. They are a whole weather system of memory and hope. A Tuesday is not just a Tuesday. It is the only Tuesday you will ever get.

So this is my free writing, my free afternoon, my free attention. I am not going to spend it on a grand argument. I am going to spend it on the small things: the hum of the refrigerator, the dust motes in a sunbeam, the way the word *home* feels different depending on who says it. If you are reading this, I hope you find a moment today to stop. Look down. Look up. Look closely. The museum is open. Admission is free. The only cost is the willingness to be here.
